title: Promises and pitfalls of artificial intelligence for legal applications
pub: Journal of Cross-disciplinary Research in Computational Law (CRCL), vol. 2 no. 2 (2024)
author: Sayash Kapoor · Peter Henderson · Arvind Narayanan

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Benchmark governance: High scores may lack workplace meaning
st.an: The supplied excerpt is bibliography-only and does not reveal the source authors’ position on whether benchmark scores establish real-world professional reliability. It reproduces a commentator’s contamination concern that is consistent with one mechanism identified by the cluster, but this is insufficient to show acceptance of the cluster’s broader governance proposition.
qs: Of the easiest problems on Codeforces, it solved 10/10 pre-2021 problems and 0/10 recent problems.

st.t: Cheaper assistance: More participation may not yield remedies
st.an: The supplied source summary contains only bibliographic references and no substantive claims, evidence, predictions, or recommendations. It therefore provides insufficient evidence to determine whether the source supports, develops, redirects, or opposes the cluster’s proposition that cheaper AI-enabled assistance may increase participation without improving remedies.

st.t: Professional evaluation: Realistic tasks complicate reproducible scoring
st.an: The supplied source material consists only of bibliography entries. Although those entries identify literature on benchmarking, predictive accuracy, hallucinations and failed AI applications, they do not reveal the source authors’ own view on whether credible evaluation must test professional task execution or how realistic tasks, automated judging and self-correction should be validated.
qs: AI and the Everything in the Whole Wide World Benchmark.
Against Predictive Optimization: On the Legitimacy of Decision-Making Algorithms that Optimize Predictive Accuracy.

st.t: Legal benchmarks: Realistic tasks expose uneven competence
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that bar-exam and generic benchmark scores do not establish practical legal competence. It materially develops that position by advocating legal-expert participation and naturalistic evaluation of real user interactions, particularly to address prompt sensitivity and construct-validity problems.
qs: So if an AI developer’s goal is to predict how well it will do on real-world legal tasks, measuring bar exam performance is simply not a suitable approach.

To improve the construct validity of current evaluations and prevent evaluations from falling prey to prompt sensitivity, researchers can conduct naturalistic evaluations of people using LLMs that closely model their use in the real world.

st.t: Legal reliability: Mitigation cannot eliminate verification
st.an: The source accepts that accurate legal inputs do not ensure reliable outputs and that failures can cause sanctions. It materially extends the cluster by advocating evaluation through expert-curated real-world tasks and user interactions, alongside clearer provider communication of limitations.
qs: Even when a language model is trained on accurate text, such as a filtered dataset of past legal documents, it is not guaranteed to produce accurate outputs [37].
Comparing the performance of these models on real-world tasks, especially those curated by legal experts, is more likely to be useful.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s rejection of autonomous lawyer substitution and materially strengthens its tool-specific approach by proposing that legal AI uses be authorized only through evaluations reflecting their intended real-world application. It also shows why demonstrations and bar-exam benchmarks do not establish lawyer-level capability, though it does not directly address verification costs or confidentiality controls.
qs: In this position paper, we argue that the kinds of legal applications we can legitimately use AI for should be determined by the evaluations that reflect said use in the real world.
Yet, this is not evidence that GPT-4 is becoming as capable as lawyers: after all, it is not a lawyer’s job to answer bar exam questions all day.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition that legal AI capability is task-specific and that safe value depends on verification and context-sensitive deployment. It materially develops that view by supplying an evaluation framework based on answerability and observability, and by recommending real-world socio-technical assessment rather than reliance on benchmark performance alone.
qs: We find that the ease of evaluating legal applications varies greatly across legal tasks, based on the ease of identifying correct answers and the observability of information relevant to the task at hand.

CONCLUSION The effective deployment of AI in legal contexts requires shifting from technical evaluations to robust socio-technical assessments carried out in the specific context in which an AI system would be deployed.

st.t: Generative automation: Fluent work product still needs authority
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s qualified view that legal AI can perform both information-processing and substantive generative tasks, while task-level success does not establish general superiority. Its central contribution is to explain that evaluation becomes less determinate for drafting, reasoning and strategy because those tasks may lack a single correct answer. It does not directly address the cluster’s separate claims about verification, authority or professional responsibility.
qs: We analyze three broad uses of AI in the legal domain: (i) tasks involving information processing, such as summarization or legal information retrieval; (ii) tasks involving creativity, reasoning, or judgment, such as preparing legal filings; and (iii) tasks involving predictions about the future, such as criminal risk prediction as well as predicting the outcomes of court decisions.

For instance, if generative AI is used to prepare a legal filing (an example of a task involving creativity, reasoning, or judgment), there is no single correct answer on how the document should be written—reasonable people can disagree on what strategies to take.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s calibrated position: AI can make legal information-processing more accessible, but evidence about lay use remains limited, factual reliability is unresolved, and consequential deployment requires close verification and context-specific evaluation rather than assumptions of lawyer-level capability.
qs: Yet, there is a paucity of evidence about how chatbots affect users who turn to them for information- processing tasks such as legal information retrieval or translation.
As a result, the outputs of language models must be closely verified before they can be used in consequential settings.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s cautious, task-specific approach: legal AI should be judged through evaluations reflecting intended real-world uses, and bar-exam performance does not establish autonomous professional competence. Its discussion of replacement rhetoric and UPL risk is consistent with the cluster but does not materially extend its reform analysis.
qs: In this position paper, we argue that the kinds of legal applications we can legitimately use AI for should be determined by the evaluations that reflect said use in the real world.
Yet, this is not evidence that GPT-4 is becoming as capable as lawyers: after all, it is not a lawyer’s job to answer bar exam questions all day.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s cautious, task-specific assessment: it distinguishes readily evaluated information processing from judgment-intensive work and finds the clearest expert gains in reduced development cost rather than transformative or established accuracy improvements. It does not directly address the cluster’s central claim about verification costs or grounding limits.
qs: For instance, if generative AI is used to prepare a legal filing (an example of a task involving creativity, reasoning, or judgment), there is no single correct answer on how the document should be written—reasonable people can disagree on what strategies to take.

For these reasons, while large language models offer improvements over existing tools — possibly in terms of accuracy but especially in terms of cost, by decreasing the amount of task-specific software development required — they do not drastically change legal information processing for experts.

st.t: Legal prediction: Classification cannot guarantee sound advice
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition by finding that most claimed court-outcome studies do not test genuine prediction, so classification-style results cannot establish practically reliable legal forecasting or advice. It also supports limiting AI to narrower, information-suitable tasks with safeguards rather than relying automatically on general outcome predictions.
qs: In sum, only 12 of 171 papers (7%) end up predicting court decisions.
Since the text of the final judgment includes the verdict, these studies do not provide real-world evidence of the usefulness of AI in judgment prediction.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source strongly aligns with the cluster’s cautious, task-specific account: it rejects unsupported profession-wide transformation claims, distinguishes readily evaluated information-processing tasks from harder judgment and prediction tasks, and endorses deployment-specific socio-technical evaluation rather than reliance on benchmarks alone. It does not directly address every cluster theme, including apprenticeship, labour markets and pricing.
qs: Tasks that would lead to the most significant changes to the legal profession are also the ones most prone to overoptimism about AI capabilities, as they are harder to evaluate.

CONCLUSION The effective deployment of AI in legal contexts requires shifting from technical evaluations to robust socio-technical assessments carried out in the specific context in which an AI system would be deployed.

kp.k: Professional transformation claims exceed current evidence
kp.d: This 2024 position paper argues that evidence does not support claims that AI is set to redefine the legal profession. The authors contrast longstanding replacement rhetoric with an eight percent increase in U.S. lawyer numbers since a 2011 newspaper headline predicting software replacement. They treat automation of consequential professional tasks as a conditional possibility, not an established outcome.
qs: Is AI set to redefine the legal profession? We argue that this claim is not supported by the current evidence.
Since the article was published, the number of lawyers in the U.S. has actually increased by eight percent [49].

kp.d: The authors distinguish information processing; creativity, reasoning or judgment; and predictions about the future. Evaluation depends on whether correct answers can be identified and relevant information observed. Tasks with potentially greater professional consequences are generally harder to evaluate and therefore more susceptible to exaggerated capability claims.
qs: We find that the ease of evaluating legal applications varies greatly across legal tasks, based on the ease of identifying correct answers and the observability of information relevant to the task at hand.
Tasks that would lead to the most significant changes to the legal profession are also the ones most prone to overoptimism about AI capabilities, as they are harder to evaluate.

kp.d: The paper reports that DoNotPay CEO Joshua Browder offered USD 1 million on January 8, 2023, for a lawyer to repeat its software's arguments through an earpiece in a U.S. Supreme Court case. It describes the Court's electronics prohibition and unauthorized-practice restrictions, followed by withdrawal of the proposal, rebranding from robot lawyer to AI consumer champion, and multiple class-action lawsuits.
qs: Even setting aside the fact that the Supreme Court prohibits electronics in the courtroom, the U.S. has several laws prohibiting the unauthorized practice of law by individuals who are not licensed attorneys.
Soon after the announcement, the CEO backed down [28], and the term ‘robot lawyer’ was changed to ‘AI consumer champion’ on the company’s website [3].

kp.k: Information processing offers incremental improvements for experts
kp.d: Legal summarization, translation, redaction, e-discovery and retrieval are comparatively amenable to evaluation because inputs and correct outputs are often observable. The authors characterize generative AI as evolutionary for legal experts: automation already existed, chatbots do not necessarily outperform law-specific fine-tuned models, and many tasks do not require a law degree. Potential benefits include accuracy improvements and especially lower task-specific software development costs.
qs: For legal experts, generative AI for information processing is an evolution, not a revolution.
Recent instruction-tuned language models (chatbots) cannot necessarily outperform models fine-tuned on law-specific datasets [12].
Further, many information-processing tasks can also be carried out by professionals without a law degree.

kp.k: Layperson benefits and harms require real-world evidence
kp.d: Natural-language interfaces enable laypeople to retrieve legal information or translate documents, but the authors identify little evidence on actual chatbot use and outcomes. They cite a 2019 U.S. survey in which 31% used the internet and 29% lawyers for legal advice, while 63% used internet information as a factor in resolving legal problems. Reported asylum-translation failures illustrate potentially catastrophic consequences; the paper recommends naturalistic research rather than assuming benefits.
qs: Yet, there is a paucity of evidence about how chatbots affect users who turn to them for information- processing tasks such as legal information retrieval or translation.
For example, asylum applications for refugees can be rejected if machine translation introduces errors because they cannot accurately infer context [16].

kp.k: Hallucinations necessitate verification and clearer warnings
kp.d: The authors describe factual unreliability as an unresolved obstacle to consequential legal deployment and require close human verification of outputs. They cite lawyer sanctions involving fabricated filing material and emphasize that training on accurate legal documents does not guarantee accurate responses. Developers should communicate these limitations more effectively; the paper reports existing product disclaimers and judicial chambers' rules as responses, not proof that the problem is solved.
qs: As a result, the outputs of language models must be closely verified before they can be used in consequential settings.
Even when a language model is trained on accurate text, such as a filtered dataset of past legal documents, it is not guaranteed to produce accurate outputs [37].
These cases highlight the need for better communication of these limitations for end users by companies providing these services [51].

kp.k: Even information-processing evaluations contain legal ambiguity
kp.d: The paper qualifies its comparatively favorable assessment: experts may disagree on multi-area classifications, translations can lack contextual equivalents, and discovery parties have opposing disclosure incentives. In Kaiser Aluminum Warrick, LLC v. US Magnesium LLC, parties disputed redaction scope and the court ordered relevant information unredacted. The authors nevertheless regard such disagreements as generally atypical, with consensus available for most information-processing tasks.
qs: Even within information- processing tasks, ease of evaluation is a spectrum.
And parties dispute how e-discovery systems are evaluated, with requesting parties generally seeking to discover more information and producing parties wanting to reveal less [22].
Nonetheless, such disagreements are generally over atypical cases, and the bulk of information processing tasks will have consensus answers when polling a larger pool of annotators.

kp.k: Bar-exam performance does not establish professional competence
kp.d: The paper reports OpenAI's claim that GPT-4 scored around the top 10% on a simulated bar exam but rejects its use as evidence of lawyer-equivalent capability. Its construct-validity critique is that exams emphasize subject knowledge over practical skills, and models can exploit memorization or shallow reasoning without demonstrating transfer to novel facts and judicial developments.
qs: Yet, this is not evidence that GPT-4 is becoming as capable as lawyers: after all, it is not a lawyer’s job to answer bar exam questions all day.
In short, tests designed for humans lack construct validity when applied to bots.
So if an AI developer’s goal is to predict how well it will do on real-world legal tasks, measuring bar exam performance is simply not a suitable approach.

kp.k: Training contamination can inflate benchmark performance
kp.d: The authors explain that overlap between training and evaluation data can reward memorization rather than generalization. They consider contamination of bar-exam evaluations possible but unproven because training and fine-tuning data are proprietary. As cross-domain illustration, they discuss GPT-4's stronger performance on Codeforces problems before its September 2021 training cutoff than afterward, while explicitly noting that OpenAI's technical-report evaluation used fresh problems and performed poorly.
qs: Contamination refers to including the same data in the training and evaluation data sets for a model [32].

It is possible that evaluations such as OpenAI’s claims about bar exam performance are overoptimistic due to contamination, but it is hard to know for sure due to the training and fine tuning data being proprietary.

kp.k: Prompt sensitivity limits transfer from benchmarks to practice
kp.d: Small prompt changes, model changes over time and differences in user expertise can substantially alter results. The authors distinguish developers' programmatic prompting, legal professionals' use, and laypeople's use: professional results may depend on prompting training, while missing naturalistic data particularly constrain evaluation of layperson interactions. They cite research finding double-digit percentage-point effects from merely reordering few-shot examples.
qs: Small changes to the prompt can significantly impact the model’s outputs [23].
Second, in use by legal professionals, prompt sensitivity means that results are conditional on users being trained on proper prompting techniques.
Even ordering few-shot examples in a prompt differently can affect performance by double-digit percentage points [31].

kp.k: Legal experts and naturalistic studies should guide evaluation
kp.d: The authors recommend involving legal experts in quantitative and qualitative evaluation to measure usefulness in actual work. They identify the interdisciplinary academic LegalBench benchmark as a constructive example but suggest qualitative observation may be even more valuable while appropriate research questions remain unsettled. At publication, they knew of no such qualitative studies of legal professionals and pointed to other professions as methodological precedents.
qs: The involvement of legal experts in designing and conducting evaluations is necessary to improve the status quo.
An interdisciplinary group of lawyers and AI experts created the LegalBench benchmark for evaluating language models on various legal reasoning tasks [23].
To our knowledge, such qualitative studies have not yet been conducted for legal professionals.

kp.k: Narrow error-checking supports augmentation rather than binding automation
kp.d: The paper favors constrained applications with well-defined outcomes and observable evidence. It reports that the Social Security Administration already uses a simple model to identify judgment errors, such as failure to address a claimant's medical claim. Citing over 86% of patent applications receiving at least one non-final rejection, it proposes semi-automated checks as a possible cost reduction for applicants and the patent office—not an established result. Recommendations should remain informative and nonbinding, with thorough appeals available.
qs: The Social Security Administration already uses a simple model to spot issues with judgments that might lead to a remand of the judgment on appeal [20].
Deployments should be structured to favour helpful, informative recommendations to both parties in a dispute rather than being used as a binding mechanism.
And a thorough appeals process should be available.

kp.k: Most claimed judgment prediction studies do not predict
kp.d: The authors report Medvedeva and Mcbride's review of 171 papers: only 12, or 7%, actually predicted court decisions. Many instead classified verdicts from judgment texts already containing the answers, inflating apparent accuracy through leakage. Genuine prediction studies had substantially lower accuracy. Missing context, jurisdictional variation, limited relevant training data and evolving judges, precedent and legislation further complicate prediction.
qs: In sum, only 12 of 171 papers (7%) end up predicting court decisions.
Since the text of the final judgment includes the verdict, these studies do not provide real-world evidence of the usefulness of AI in judgment prediction.
Moreover, for the small minority of papers that actually predict court outcomes, the accuracy of the resulting models is much lower.

kp.k: Judgment prediction should not determine legal outcomes
kp.d: The authors distinguish carefully evaluated assistance that flags common brief errors from systems making decisions or final recommendations to decision-makers. They support the former only as optional attorney guidance and reject the latter. This restriction follows from evaluation shortcomings, possible bias and input sensitivity, rather than a claim that reliable general-purpose adjudication has been demonstrated.
qs: This would serve as a suggestion to attorneys that might miss common errors but not result in any binding outcome and could be ignored by the attorney.
On the other hand, such systems should not be used to make decisions or final recommendations to a decision-maker.

kp.k: Recidivism tools illustrate accuracy, fairness and transfer failures
kp.d: The paper reports that ProPublica's 2016 COMPAS investigation found twice as many false positives for Black defendants as White defendants and overall accuracy around 65%; Dressel and Farid subsequently found performance no better than predictions by people without criminal-justice backgrounds. It also reports that PSA, used in over half of U.S. states and trained on 1.5 million cases, faced a Cook County violent-recidivism rate ten times lower than its nationwide training data. These examples support the authors' concerns about unobservable personal circumstances and distribution shift.
qs: Perhaps more surprisingly, the investigation found that the overall accuracy of the algorithm was only around 65%.
In a follow-up study, Dressel and Farid [18] found that this accuracy was no more accurate than predictions made by people without any background in criminal justice.
Corey [15] highlights that in Cook County, Illinois, the rate of violent recidivism is ten times lower than the nationwide data that was used for training PSA.

kp.k: Vendor opacity weakens accountability and contestability
kp.d: The authors argue that predictive-AI vendors promise automation but invoke human-use qualifications when tools fail, diffusing responsibility across stakeholders. Trade-secret claims impede challenges by affected people, while courts' purchase of generic rather than locally tailored products exacerbates evaluation problems. They recommend stronger developer transparency, contestability mechanisms and assessment of societal effects, citing an eight-application cross-domain analysis as evidence that these issues extend beyond criminal justice.
qs: Vendors sell predictive AI based on the promise of full automation and elimination of jobs, but when it performs poorly, they retreat to the fine print, which says that the tool should not be used on its own.
The individual decisions made by these systems also tend not to be contestable by decision subjects, as vendors claim that the logic of the tool is a trade secret [26, 38].

This requires much stronger transparency by the developers, clear mechanisms to ensure contestability to decision subjects, and evaluations that go beyond just the technical specifications of these tools into the societal impact of these tools.

kp.d: The paper's overarching recommendation is to move beyond technical performance measures toward assessment of the particular institutional and social setting of deployment. The authors acknowledge costs but regard these assessments as necessary given legal complexity and societal consequences. Appropriate uses should follow from credible evaluation, rather than impressive demonstrations or generalized benchmark scores.
qs: The effective deployment of AI in legal contexts requires shifting from technical evaluations to robust socio-technical assessments carried out in the specific context in which an AI system would be deployed.
To answer the question ‘What can I use an AI system for?’, it is essential first to answer ‘How was this AI system evaluated?’.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Kapoor, Henderson and Narayanan argue that current evidence does not establish that AI will redefine or replace the legal profession.
pts.d: The authors distinguish established information-processing applications from hypothetical automation of expert judgment and problematic future-outcome prediction. They argue that applications with the greatest potential professional impact are also harder to evaluate and especially vulnerable to overoptimism. This is an assessment of the evidence available in early 2024, not a prediction that substantial change can never occur. DoNotPay's robot-lawyer promotion and OpenAI's bar-exam claims are examples they scrutinize, not claims they endorse.

pts.k: Generative AI offers incremental improvements to expert legal information processing, particularly lower software-development costs, rather than a wholesale revolution.
pts.d: The authors identify summarization, translation, redaction, e-discovery and information retrieval as comparatively tractable applications. They argue that existing automation, the availability of specialized models and the fact that many such tasks do not require a law degree limit the novelty of LLMs for legal experts. They do not quantify productivity gains, cost savings or employment effects.

pts.k: Natural-language interfaces make legal information tasks available to laypeople, but their real-world benefits remain uncertain and errors can cause serious harm.
pts.d: The authors describe opportunities for translation and finding relevant legal rules, while emphasizing the lack of evidence about everyday chatbot use. They identify rejected asylum applications as a potential consequence of translation errors. This is not a demonstrated claim that chatbots close the justice gap.

pts.k: Fabricated output remains a barrier to consequential legal use and creates a need for close human verification.
pts.d: The authors state that factual reliability remains unresolved, including for models trained on accurate legal text. They link unrecognized fabrication to professional harm and sanctions, recommending clearer communication of limitations. The cited sanctions incidents are examples of harm, not measurements of hallucination rates.

pts.k: Automating expert drafting or judgment could have a large professional impact, but existing benchmarks do not establish that capability.
pts.d: Preparing filings, mediation and dispute resolution are presented as potentially transformative applications only if automation proves effective. The authors argue that contamination, inadequate construct validity and prompt sensitivity undermine extrapolation from benchmark scores to client service. They suggest that shallow reasoning may suffice for constrained uses such as bar preparation, while new facts and judicial decisions pose different demands.

pts.k: Narrow, observable error-checking applications offer a concrete opportunity for assistance and possible cost reduction.
pts.d: The authors describe an existing Social Security Administration system that flags problems in benefits decisions, such as failure to address a medical claim. They propose extending similar checks to filings, including patent applications, to reduce costs for applicants and the USPTO. The cost reduction is a proposed benefit, not a measured result. Their preferred model is nonbinding assistance with appeal rights, not autonomous adjudication.

pts.k: Published court-outcome prediction results substantially overstate demonstrated usefulness; any defensible use should be limited to nonbinding assistance.
pts.d: The authors identify potential value for legal strategy and litigation-risk assessment but argue that most published systems classify information already containing the outcome rather than predict future judgments. Genuine prediction is harder because context is incomplete, jurisdictions differ and judges, precedent and legislation change. They recommend using adequately evaluated systems to flag common briefing errors, not to make decisions or final recommendations to decision-makers.

pts.k: Predictive AI used for detention, parole and other decisions about people has shortcomings that may negate its promised benefits.
pts.d: The authors attribute failures to limited observability of people's circumstances, distribution shift, weak accountability, trade secrecy and generic vendor products insufficiently adapted to local populations. They call for stronger transparency, contestability and societal-impact evaluation. Their discussion concerns predictive systems, not exclusively generative language models.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The overarching argument is a position-paper synthesis of published research, historical employment figures and deployment examples, rather than a new labour-market or productivity study.
pts.d: The authors contrast a 2011 newspaper headline about replacing lawyers with software against an eight-percent increase in US lawyer numbers since publication, citing a statistical series covering 2007–2022. They also describe DoNotPay's withdrawal of its proposed courtroom demonstration and ensuing lawsuits. Their central methodological argument is that test performance does not establish competence in actual legal practice.

pts.k: The information-processing assessment rests on prior automation, a cited legal benchmark comparison and the relative evaluability of these tasks.
pts.d: The authors cite legal summarization tools existing for more than a decade and Chalkidis's work on ChatGPT and LexGLUE. They use Learned Hands as an example of comparing model classifications with lawyer labels. Their argument is that these applications generally have identifiable correct answers and observable relevant inputs, enabling evidence-based deployment; they acknowledge exceptions involving ambiguity and contested labels.

pts.k: Evidence about lay users includes pre-chatbot legal-information behaviour and reporting on asylum translation errors, not a direct evaluation of current chatbot outcomes.
pts.d: The authors report that a 2019 US survey found 31% used the internet for legal advice versus 29% using lawyers, and 63% used internet information in resolving legal problems. They cite reporting on Afghan asylum claims for translation harms and explicitly call for naturalistic evaluations of chatbot users.

pts.k: The authors support their benchmark critique with contamination examples, exam-design criticisms and prompt-sensitivity research, while acknowledging uncertainty about GPT-4's training data.
pts.d: They use pre- versus post-training-cutoff Codeforces performance as a cross-domain illustration of possible memorization, not direct proof of bar-exam contamination. They cite criticism of the bar exam's emphasis on subject knowledge and research showing double-digit percentage-point changes from reordering prompt examples. LegalBench is identified as a collaboratively developed academic benchmark that improves professional involvement, but does not remove all concerns about real-world use.

pts.k: The court-prediction critique principally relies on Medvedeva and McBride's review of 171 papers.
pts.d: The authors report that only 12 papers, or 7%, actually predicted court decisions. They connect the review to earlier research by Medvedeva and colleagues and to the broader problem of data leakage. No pooled accuracy figure for the genuine prediction studies is supplied.

pts.k: The predictive-AI argument draws on reported COMPAS performance, a follow-up comparison with laypeople, local PSA distribution differences and a cross-domain review.
pts.d: The authors cite ProPublica's 2016 investigation as finding approximately 65% COMPAS accuracy and twice as many false positives for Black defendants as White defendants. They cite Dressel and Farid's 2018 study as finding no accuracy advantage over people without criminal-justice expertise. For PSA, they report training on 1.5 million national cases and a Cook County violent-recidivism rate ten times lower than in its training data, drawing on Corey. Wang and colleagues' analysis of eight predictive-AI applications supports their wider institutional critique.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Claims concern the evidence and deployments available by early 2024; future benefits are conditional and have no specified delivery date.
pts.d: The authors set no timeline for lawyer replacement, broad automation or cost savings. Information-processing deployment depends on robust evaluation and verification. Expert-task benefits remain hypothetical; professional performance depends partly on prompting skills and may change as models change. Narrow error checking requires well-defined issues and access to relevant evidence. Across applications, they require context-specific socio-technical assessment rather than relying only on technical benchmarks.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The source differentiates professional users, lay users, public adjudicators, applicants and people subject to predictive decisions.
pts.d: Legal professionals may gain incremental information-processing support and error detection but must verify output and face professional consequences from fabricated filings. Laypeople may obtain easier access to legal information while lacking the expertise to recognize errors; asylum seekers illustrate high-stakes exposure. Benefits adjudicators, patent applicants and the USPTO could benefit from narrow checks. Lawyers and businesses are potential users of litigation forecasts, whose practical value the authors question. Criminal defendants face liberty consequences, racial disparities and difficulty contesting proprietary tools. Developers and court purchasers bear responsibilities for evaluation, disclosure and appropriate deployment. The paper does not forecast effects by law-firm size, staffing structure or billing model.
